formal_status: Christmas Day is listed as a federal holiday on the Office of Personnel Management federal-holiday schedule.
observed_practice: The federal work calendar therefore closes for most federal employees around a holiday explicitly named Christmas Day, subject to the statutory rules for weekend observance.
interpretation: This documents Christian-origin terminology embedded in a federal civic calendar. It is not evidence that the United States has an official religion.
scope_note: This record concerns the federal employee holiday calendar, not every state, school, court, or private employer calendar.

formal_status: Easter is not listed as a federal employee holiday on the OPM federal-holiday schedule.
observed_practice: The White House continues an official Easter Egg Roll tradition dating to 1878; the 2026 event was held on April 6, 2026.
interpretation: This is evidence of Christian-origin cultural visibility in official government practice without federal-holiday status. The event is presented as a civic and family tradition rather than compelled religious observance.

sources.label: White House — 2026 Easter Egg Roll announcement

scope_note: An official tradition can show cultural visibility without creating a legal obligation to observe the underlying religion.

formal_status: Congress added “under God” to the Pledge of Allegiance in 1954; federal legislation required “In God We Trust” on currency in 1955 and established it as the national motto in 1956.
observed_practice: Religious language remains present in recurring federal civic symbols and currency.
interpretation: These are explicit government religious references. Their presence is analytically separate from whether the federal government establishes an official religion.

sources.label: U.S. House History — currency motto legislation

scope_note: This record documents official language and symbols; constitutional doctrine concerning ceremonial religious language is a separate legal question.

formal_status: Article VI of the U.S. Constitution bars a religious test as a qualification for federal office or public trust.
observed_practice: Pew reported that Christians made up 87% of voting members expected in the 119th Congress at its January 2025 convening, compared with 62% of U.S. adults; less than 1% of Congress was categorized as religiously unaffiliated, compared with 28% of U.S. adults.
interpretation: This establishes a dated representation difference. It does not establish why the difference exists and is not evidence of an informal religious test by itself.

sources.label: Pew — Religious Composition of the 119th Congress

scope_note: The congressional figures describe Pew's January 2025 roster analysis and should not be presented as a continuously updated membership count.

formal_status: Current U.S. Department of Education guidance says public schools may teach about religion and religious holidays but may not observe holidays as religious events or promote student religious observance.
observed_practice: The same 2026 federal guidance recognizes religious excusals and accommodations in defined circumstances, including prayer, religious exercise, and religiously motivated requests for excusal.
interpretation: This is an accommodation framework. Whether a particular district's default calendar or practice advantages one tradition requires district-specific evidence rather than a national assumption.

sources.label: U.S. Department of Education — 2026 prayer and religious-expression guidance

scope_note: Department guidance summarizes the federal constitutional baseline; state law and local policy may add requirements or accommodations.
